chapter: Maple Leaf, own orchestra and rivals
title: Red Dugas, Henry Martin and the need for a lively drummer
summary: Charles recalls Red Dugas quitting after teasing and says a drummer must be lively, citing Cottrell and Welch.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Red Dugas played with me when I first started, when I first put up the band. But somehow they criticized him so much, I said poor Red, he quit himself. Is that right?
They kind of teased him or something? Criticized him? Yeah.

They criticized Red so much, those boys, about he couldn't play, you know. In other words, Red couldn't produce the good like some of them drummers, and they criticized him. So Red got hot and he just left. And first thing you know Red then the little, what do you call him, piano, I mean that violin

player. Welch. Welch. You know something I don't understand about Henry Martin now. You remember Alfred Williams, a drummer, he's always talking about how great Henry Martin was you know, and what a wonderful drummer he was. Why did he switch to banjo? No, no.

Henry Martin couldn't play no drums. No? No. He played the drum. You know a drummer, not to say talk about it, but a drummer, he's got to be fast. A drummer can't lag. A drummer can make you play music. Or you can play if you've got a drummer. That's right. Oh my goodness. That's why my band used to run. One Red was playing with me that was a dead band. But when Welch got in there, but look when we had the Maple Leaf band, Cantrell was playing in there. You talk about a drummer.

Set it on fire. Oh yes indeed. Because otherwise, you know, in playing drums you've got to have somebody that's lively, very lively. Just like I'm talking about that old man playing that bass drum that went on to Garnier. Never heard of such a thing in my life.
